newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines' Ramos repeats vow to relinquish power.
newsitem.headline: Philippines' Ramos repeats vow to relinquish power.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos on Tuesday repeated his vow to relinquish power next year as the nation commemorated the 1986 revolt that ended the rule of strongman Ferdinand Marcos.
This year's celebration has been clouded by a controversy over calls from Ramos's supporters to change the constitution and allow him to stay in power after his six-year term ends in June 1998.
Marcos stayed in power for 20 years before being forced to flee the country.

Ramos renewed his pledge to step down in a speech. He said one of his remaining goals was to reduce poverty from around 40 percent "to 30 percent by 1998 -- the year when I relinquish my watch on the presidency".

The celebration was held at a monument built on a corner of Manila's Edsa highway where a million civilians massed in 1986 to protect Ramos, then defence minister Juan Ponce Enrile and 300 army mutineers from advancing Marcos tanks.
Marcos fled to Hawaii at the height of the four-day people power revolt and died there in exile three years later.

Cardinal Jaime Sin, the Philippines' most influential churchman and a key rallying figure during the Edsa revolt, has been among Ramos's most severe critics since the controversy over his term in office began.
But on Tuesday he praised Ramos for reiterating his commitment to step down.

"Happily, the president has repeatedly denied interest in another term...He has refused to sully the limited legitimacy of his incumbency with the unlimited shamelessness of a megalomaniac despot," Sin said in the text of a prepared homily he was to deliver later on Tuesday.
But the Manila archbishop, clearly referring to presidential advisers, attacked "the dubious forces" that he said were trying to convince Ramos to change his mind.
Sin said democracy should not be taken for granted, warning, "it can fall prey to a deluded ruler".
Sin and former president Corazon Aquino joined Ramos in the celebration of the 11th anniversary of the uprising that catapulted Aquino to power.
Aquino said on Monday she was convinced Ramos was sincere in his promise to step down but urged him to dispel all doubts by arranging for "a peaceful transfer of power" to his successor.
About 300 children, born around the time the uprising broke out, joined Ramos, Sin and Aquino in the celebration, carrying a sign reading: "Edsa Babies."
The Philippine Daily Inquirer newspaper said the 1986 revolt had fallen short of its promise, noting that Marcos's wife, Imelda, and the couple's associates were back in power as members of congress.

"Up to now there has been no restitution, no retribution, no punishment," it said in an editorial. "The billions stolen from public coffers have not been returned. Justice still has to be done to the people, and specially to the victims of human rights violations of the Marcos dictatorship."
